title: Databricks gateway: list Unity Catalog model services and send their UC names
description:
## Summary

On Unity AI Gateway workspaces, the Databricks provider now lists models from the Unity Catalog model-services API and sends each model's Unity Catalog name to the gateway.
This fixes newer gateway-only models failing and makes custom `catalog.schema.service` routes show up in the model picker.

Addresses the last two comments on posit-dev/assistant#2231.

## What was broken and how it's fixed

| What wasn't working | How we fixed it | How it's been checked so far |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Newer gateway-only models failed. Picking DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 returned `403 PERMISSION_DENIED ... available only via Unity Gateway`, because we sent the old `databricks-*` name. | On the gateway, we send the Unity Catalog name (`system.ai.deepseek-v4-1-flash-1017`) in every chat request. | blairj09 confirmed with curl on AWS and Azure that UC names return 200 on every gateway route (unified Responses and chat, Anthropic, OpenAI Responses, Gemini). Positron test (below). |
| Custom `catalog.schema.service` routes never showed up, because the model list came from the foundation-models API, which only has Databricks' own models. | The gateway model list now comes from `GET /api/2.1/unity-catalog/model-services` with no `parent` (every service the user can access) and `view=FULL`. Custom routes are listed under their full three-part name. | Unit tests with custom-route data based on blairj09's Azure test services. |
| `/api/ai-gateway/v2/endpoints` couldn't replace the model list: it's missing 17 newer models, and the names it returns give 404. | Not used for the list. It's still used only to check whether the workspace has the gateway. | Confirmed by blairj09. |
| Routes were guessed from older fields (`served_entities`, `api_types`), which model services don't have. | Each model's route comes from the `supported_api_types` it lists. Claude still uses Anthropic Messages, GPT uses OpenAI Responses, Gemini uses generateContent, and other models use unified Responses or chat. Models with no chat or Responses route (embeddings) are left out. | Unit tests for each route. Positron test with Claude, GPT, Gemini and DeepSeek (below). |
| Gemini's native route was never used. We expected `gemini/v1beta/generateContent`, but Databricks lists `gemini/v1/generateContent` and `gemini/v1/streamGenerateContent`. | Require `gemini/v1/streamGenerateContent`, since chat always streams. A service that only lists the non-streaming type falls back to unified Responses. The request path stays `/ai-gateway/gemini/v1beta/...`. | Real captured response, plus blairj09's 200 on the `v1beta` request path. Positron test: Gemini 3.5 Flash replied over its own route (below). |
| `supported_api_types` is `null` for custom services unless you ask for `view=FULL`. | Always request `view=FULL`. | Real captured response (system models). blairj09 confirmed the custom-service case on Azure. |
| Paging: an empty page can still have a `next_page_token`, so an empty page doesn't mean the list is done. | Keep fetching until there's no token. Also stop and warn if a token repeats, warn if the 50-page cap cuts the list short, and skip duplicate services. | Unit tests, including an empty page with a token. |
| Model services don't have display names. | Use the foundation-models display name when the model matches (so "Claude Sonnet 4.6" still shows), otherwise the bare name (`deepseek-v4-1-flash-1017`). Custom routes show their full name. If the foundation-models request fails, is slow (5-second limit) or returns bad data, the list still loads with bare names. | Unit tests, including failed, malformed and hanging responses. Positron test: names showed correctly in the picker (below). |
| Changing model ids would break saved selections, conversations, `defaultModel` and allow/deny lists from earlier releases. | System models keep their `databricks-*` id in the list and in config, and only the gateway request uses `system.ai.*`. That includes a config override URL pointing at this workspace's own `/ai-gateway/`. Any other override URL (for example a proxy) gets the id unchanged. | Unit tests for the name change on the gateway, serving, own-gateway override and proxy override paths. Positron test: a conversation saved earlier with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 still showed that model (below). |

## Not fixed

Retired models still show up. For example, `deepseek-v4-1-flash` is listed but returns `400 ... is deprecated`, and nothing in either Databricks list marks it as retired.
The chat does show Databricks' full error message, which says the model is deprecated and links to the supported models.
Tracked in posit-dev/assistant#2997.

## Tested in Positron

Tested on AWS databricks with a dev build of this branch in Positron.
Discovery listed 52 chat models from the Unity AI Gateway (56 services, minus 3 embedding models and 1 non-chat service).

| Model | Result | Name sent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (gateway-only, used to fail with 403) | Replied | `system.ai.deepseek-v4-1-flash-1017` |
| Claude Sonnet 5.5 | Replied | `system.ai.claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| GPT-6 Luna | Replied | `system.ai.gpt-6-luna` |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash | Replied over Gemini's own route (request used Gemini's `contents` format) | `system.ai.gemini-3-5-flash` |
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (retired) | Failed as expected, showing Databricks' message: `HTTP 400: BAD_REQUEST: This endpoint databricks-deepseek-v4-1-flash is deprecated...` | `system.ai.deepseek-v4-1-flash` |

Display names from the foundation-models list showed in the picker (for example "Claude Sonnet 5.5", "GLM 5.3"). A conversation and remembered model saved earlier with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 still showed that model when Positron opened.

## Tested on Azure

blairj09 tested e6cc8e2 directly against ai-lib (not through the picker) with three custom routes on an Azure workspace:

| Route | Behind it | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `posit_test_claude` | Claude Sonnet 4.6 | Listed, chat and tool calls worked. Didn't get the Anthropic route even though it lists it, as intended. |
| `posit_test_fallback` | Claude Sonnet 4.6, falling back to GPT-OSS 120B | Listed, chat and tool calls worked (Claude answered). |
| `posit_test_gptoss` | GPT-OSS 120B | Listed and chat worked, but tool calls came back with empty arguments (`{}`). Fixed since, see below. |

`view=FULL` returned `supported_api_types` for all three, and discovery listed them under their full three-part names.

## Still needs testing

| Check | What it confirms | How to test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retest tool calls on the three Azure custom routes with 6d7c9e8 | Custom routes now use chat completions, so GPT-OSS sends real tool-call arguments, and Claude still works over chat completions. | Run a tool call on `posit_test_claude`, `posit_test_fallback` and `posit_test_gptoss`. |
| Custom routes in the model picker | They show up and can be picked in Positron and RStudio. | Open the picker on the Azure workspace. |
| RStudio | The same results as Positron. | Repeat the Positron test in RStudio. |
| A multi-page model-services list (low priority) | Paging works on a real response. Paging logic is covered by unit tests. | Needs a workspace with more than 100 model services. |

## Test data

Test data is written by hand, based on a real `view=FULL` response from `rstudio-partner-posit-default` and blairj09's Azure notes.

## Also fixed during review

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| A custom route whose name starts like a known model (for example `gpt-5.team.router`) was treated as that model and got its native route and limits. | Custom routes are treated as unknown models: they use chat or unified Responses (whichever they list) and default limits, never a vendor's own route. |
| A custom route whose catalog starts with `databricks-` (for example `databricks-team.catalog.router`) would have been renamed to `system.ai.team.catalog.router`. | Only rename when the rest of the name has no dots. System model names never have dots, and custom route names always do. |
| If the model-services list failed (for example on an older or restricted workspace), the gateway would list no models at all. | Fall back to the foundation-models list, as before this PR. Custom routes are missing in that case, but the `databricks-*` ids still get their Unity Catalog names on requests. |
| Model discovery could wait forever on a stuck page. | Discovery now uses the shared model-list cache, which stops after 15 seconds and falls back to the last list. |
| An override URL on this workspace's gateway wasn't recognized if it had an uppercase host or `:443`, so it got the old `databricks-*` name. | Parse the URL and compare its origin and `/ai-gateway/` path. |
| Custom routes avoided being matched to a known model only because the classifier keeps an empty name. | The classifier now has an explicit flag for services whose model is unknown. |
| A custom route backed by GPT-OSS (directly or as a fallback) sent tool calls with empty arguments, because GPT-OSS streams them empty over unified Responses and our GPT-OSS check matches on the model name, which custom routes don't have. | Custom routes use chat completions when they list it, and unified Responses only when it's their only route. |

## Accepted costs

- On the gateway, a model id like `databricks-<name>` (no dots) is sent as `system.ai.<name>`. A custom model in someone's config that points at their own classic serving endpoint named `databricks-*` would break on the gateway. We think this is rare.
- The picker and config keep showing `databricks-*` ids, even for gateway-only models that Databricks only lists as `system.ai.*`.
- Custom routes never use a vendor's own route or limits, even when the model behind them is known to be Claude, GPT or Gemini, because model services don't say which model is behind a route. For example, a custom route in front of Claude Sonnet 4.6 that lists `anthropic/v1/messages` still uses chat completions with a 128k context limit, so it loses Claude's prompt caching and thinking controls. Users can set `protocol` and limits for that model in providers.json. posit-dev/ai-lib#62 would make the features follow a changed `protocol` automatically.
- Custom routes on chat completions don't show reasoning text, even if the model behind them produces it. They don't get thinking controls, so we never ask for reasoning anyway.

title: Log where Google Vertex credentials come from
description:
- addresses posit-dev/positron#16254
- companion to https://github.com/posit-dev/assistant/pull/2969

Make Google Vertex credential problems diagnosable from the logs. A customer's connection failed because `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` pointed at a file that no longer existed, and nothing in the logs said so. As Positron's authentication extension stops resolving Vertex credentials, this resolution happens in ai-lib, so the logging belongs here.

The Vertex model fetcher now logs where the credential came from once a token is minted (`[GoogleVertex] Using ...`), and includes the same description in the auth-error and network-error logs. For Application Default Credentials it names the `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` path and whether the file exists, or gcloud's well-known file, or says that only the metadata server is left. The well-known file lookup mirrors google-auth-library's (`%APPDATA%\gcloud` on Windows, `~/.config/gcloud` elsewhere). Paths will show up in logs and diagnostic reports.

Before this, a missing key file surfaced as `ENOENT` and was reported as a `network_error`, so the customer's case would have been labelled a network problem. The fetcher now treats any failure as an `auth_error` when `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` points at a file that doesn't exist, since that file is the cause whatever error google-auth-library throws. Other ADC failures are classified as before: known auth messages (`invalid_grant`, expired or revoked tokens, no default credentials) are auth errors, and everything else, including proxy and TLS failures, stays a `network_error`.

A missing `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` file now gets its own status code, `adc_file_missing`, with a message naming the path, instead of `adc_expired` and advice to run `gcloud auth application-default login` (which doesn't help when the variable points at a deleted file). Other ADC failures still send `adc_expired`. posit-dev/assistant uses the new code to show the problem on the provider row and in the Vertex Edit dialog.

Not included: google-auth-library also honours a lowercase `google_application_credentials`, which credential capture doesn't declare or scrub. That gap predates this PR and is left for a separate change.

## Verification

Regression tests cover a missing `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` file (the real `ENOENT` shape, reported as an `adc_file_missing` auth error naming the path, with no success log), a transient ADC mint failure (network error that still names the source), a proxy 407 during ADC minting (network error, not expired credentials), the success log for a captured path, and each ADC description case against real temp files. The missing-file and proxy tests failed before the fix. `check-types` and `format:check` pass. Not verified against a live Vertex project.

Known gap: an ADC refresh that fails with `invalid_client` still shows as a network error, as it did before this PR.

title: Renew short-lived OAuth tokens at half-life, not on every read
description:
When a token endpoint issues access tokens that last about 2 minutes or less, the acquisition engine treats each new token as already expiring and refreshes it on every read. In Positron, each refresh also fires credential-change events whose follow-up reads refresh again, so a Posit Connect server issuing 5-second tokens received 838 refreshes in about 20 seconds after sign-in.

This PR makes a token due for renewal only once its remaining life is below the smaller of the existing fixed margin (4–6 minutes on read, 2 minutes inside the refresh lock) and half the life it had when the engine first saw it. The same rule covers the ordinary read check, the re-check inside the refresh lock, and the client-credentials cache, so the three can't drift apart. Long-lived tokens are unaffected.

The engine keeps one in-memory record per stored sign-in or client-credentials cache entry: the access token, its exact expiry, and when the engine first saw it. Because the record is keyed on first observation rather than on tokens this engine issued, it also covers tokens another window wrote, tokens loaded after a restart, and the first read after sign-in. A new token with an unchanged expiry (a server capping rotating tokens at a session end) counts as a new issuance. A token first seen near expiry renews at half its remaining life rather than immediately. Offline serving and the re-read after a failed refresh still use plain expiry, and the stored credential format is unchanged.

## Verification

New tests (fake clock) cover a freshly refreshed 5-second token being reused until half-life and then renewed once, two engines sharing a store without alternating renewals, another window's fresh token found inside the refresh lock, a capped expiry, and a short-lived client-credentials token. All of them fail on the previous code. Two existing tests that seeded a token inside the fixed margin now advance the clock past half-life and keep their failure, backoff, and offline assertions.

title: Fix a flaky Connect Bedrock abort test
description:
"aborts a Mantle listing that never answers when discovery is cancelled" failed on CI for #136 with `expected undefined to be defined`, then passed on a rerun. The test waited a fixed 1000 event-loop turns for the Bedrock model request to start. Request signing runs before that request, so on a slow CI runner the test could run out of turns before the request was sent.

The fetch stubs now resolve a promise when the request arrives, and the tests wait on that instead of counting turns. The two region re-read tests used the same loop through a helper, so they get the same change and the helper is gone.

Only test code changes.

title: Connect Bedrock: discover and chat with models through the gateway
description:
## Summary

Lets the Posit Connect provider list and chat with Amazon Bedrock models through the Connect LLM Gateway. Part of rstudio/rstudio-pro#12635.

- Sign Connect Bedrock chats with minted AWS keys in the integration's region. Resolve the runtime endpoint from the environment and forward the FIPS allowance.
- Discover models through the gateway's control plane instead of a fixed list. This includes non-Anthropic text models and Bedrock Mantle (OpenAI) models. Retired and non-chat models are skipped, and models expose their bare name.
- Report per-integration discovery state to hosts. Hide Mantle models under FIPS. Share Bedrock capability defaults between the direct and Connect providers.

## Notes

- If `ListFoundationModels` fails, the error propagates and no models are listed, as in the direct Bedrock provider.
- The assistant PR pins this branch. If this PR is squash-merged, the pin needs a bump to the merged SHA.

## Testing

`npx vitest run` and `tsc --noEmit` in `packages/ai-provider-bridge`.

title: Report when a model listing shows the API key was rejected
description:
This PR lets an app find out whether a provider rejected the API key while it listed models, so the app can tell the user. Before, a rejected key was swallowed: the listing fell back to the cached or built-in models, and the app kept showing the provider as connected. For Anthropic, whose built-in list is empty, the models simply disappeared.

Each fresh listing now reports one of three results alongside the models: the key was accepted, the key was rejected, or nothing was learned. The existing model-listing calls return the same models as before, so current callers are unaffected. A new `discoverModels` call on the provider registry returns the models and the result together.

A listing reports "rejected" when the provider answers HTTP 401. A stale cache still serves its models in that case, and the listing still reports "rejected", because the key was revoked after an earlier success. Gemini reports a bad key as HTTP 400 with an `API_KEY_INVALID` message, so Gemini also counts that as a rejection.

A listing reports "nothing learned" whenever it can't say anything about the key: a timeout, a network error, a server error, a cache hit, or a request sent without a key (Anthropic allows anonymous listing). It also reports this for providers that use their own listing path. HTTP 403 is deliberately not a rejection, because a key can be valid for chat but not allowed to list models.

The Posit Assistant PR that shows "API key rejected" on provider rows depends on this change.

title: Use Databricks' authorization-server metadata for OIDC discovery
description:
Changes how `ai-credentials` finds a Databricks workspace's OAuth endpoints for browser sign-in, to match Positron's Databricks provider (posit-dev/positron#15508) and Databricks docs.

- Discovery reads `<host>/oidc/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` instead of `<host>/.well-known/openid-configuration`. The Databricks [Go](https://github.com/databricks/databricks-sdk-go/blob/main/credentials/u2m/endpoint_supplier.go) and [Python](https://github.com/databricks/databricks-sdk-py/blob/main/databricks/sdk/oauth.py) SDKs read the same URL.
- Discovery times out after 2 seconds.
- If discovery fails (timeout, HTTP error, missing fields, or an endpoint on another origin), sign-in uses `<host>/oidc/v1/authorize` and `<host>/oidc/v1/token`, the workspace endpoints in [Databricks' U2M docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/auth/oauth-u2m). A network error or a cross-origin endpoint used to fail sign-in.
- `ai-credentials` caches the result per workspace for the life of the process, including the fallback; Positron caches only discovered endpoints. Every credential read builds the grant, so retrying a failed discovery would add up to 2 seconds to each read.

Also adds a test that a refresh response without a `refresh_token` keeps the stored one.

Part of posit-dev/assistant#2740.

title: Add OpenRouter to provider mapping
description:
## Summary

On Positron, a provider is listed only if it has an entry in `PROVIDER_MAP`. OpenRouter didn't have one, so Positron marked it `unsupported`, left it out of auth status, and never showed it. This PR adds the missing mapping, plus a test so the next new provider can't miss one the same way.

Part of posit-dev/assistant#2749.

## Changes

- **[provider-map.ts](packages/ai-provider-bridge/src/provider-map.ts):** adds `openrouter: { scopes: [], credentialType: "apikey" }`. It's a plain API-key provider, the same shape as `deepseek`.
- **[provider-map.test.ts](packages/ai-provider-bridge/src/__tests__/provider-map.test.ts):** new test that every ID in `PROVIDER_IDS` has a `PROVIDER_MAP` entry, except local providers (`LOCAL_PROVIDER_IDS`) and `copilot`, which is reached only through vscode.lm. This enforces the rule CLAUDE.md already states, which nothing checked before.
- **[providerGuide.md](memory-bank/providerGuide.md):** the Files Summary row for `provider-map.ts` now names `copilot` as an exception too, so it matches the test and CLAUDE.md.

## Context

The provider sign-in rules from posit-dev/assistant#2603 are already on Assistant's main. Under them, a mapped provider that Positron's auth extension doesn't register is stored by Assistant, the way DeepSeek and OpenCode already work. So after the pin bump, this mapping should be all OpenRouter needs to appear on Positron.

Follow-up in Assistant (not in this PR):
- Bump the `packages/ai-lib` pin.
- Remove "(not yet available in Positron)" from the OpenRouter row in `providers.mdx`.

This may also fix posit-dev/positron#14477. Positron's headless language model service registers only `MAPPED_PROVIDER_IDS`, so OpenRouter should now show up there as well.

## Testing

- `npm test -w ai-provider-bridge`
- `npm run check-types`
- `npm run format:check`
- Pointed Assistant's `packages/ai-lib` submodule at this branch and launched a dev build of Positron. OpenRouter showed up as a provider, I signed in with an API key, and I ran a chat turn with an OpenRouter model.

title: Add a headless contract version and guard
description:
Adds `HEADLESS_CONTRACT_VERSION` to the headless entry. Positron will use Posit Assistant's copy of the entry only when this number matches the copy compiled into Positron, and fall back to its own copy otherwise (posit-dev/positron#16952). The number changes only on breaking changes, so Positron keeps using Assistant's copy through additive changes.

- Adds a typecheck guard that freezes the v1 contract and fails when a change to the entry's runtime exports breaks it. Additive changes pass.
- Runs the `typechecks/` guards in CI. They weren't running before, so this also starts enforcing the existing shape guards, which pass today.

title: Let ACP agents be turned off without deleting them
description:
This PR adds an optional `enabled` setting to each Agent Client Protocol (ACP) agent in `providers.json`, so a user or admin can keep an agent configured but turned off. Before, an ACP agent was on exactly when its entry existed, so the only way to turn one off was to delete its configuration.

An agent is on unless it sets `enabled: false`, so existing files behave as before. The schema description and the docs say the same.

The resolved config also now reports which layer defined each ACP agent (user, workspace or admin, as for the other engine settings). A higher layer's entry still replaces a lower one whole, so its `enabled` and every other field come from that layer. This lets an app tell the user where an agent comes from, for example that an admin defined it and the user can't remove it.

Provenance looks up agent ids by their own keys only. An agent id such as `constructor` exists on every plain object, and without this check it would be credited to layers that never defined it.

https://github.com/posit-dev/assistant/pull/2912 depends on this change.

title: Add responseSchema for provider-enforced structured output
description:
🤖 Written by AI 🤖

This PR adds an optional `responseSchema` request parameter so a caller can require the provider to constrain the response to a JSON schema, instead of relying on prompt instructions and parsing free-text JSON. The first consumer is the assistant's auto-mode safety classifier (companion PR in posit-dev/assistant).

Each client maps the schema to its route's enforcement mechanism through the AI SDK's structured-output support: native response formats where the route has them (Anthropic `output_config`, OpenAI `json_schema`, Gemini `responseSchema`), or the SDK's schema-forced JSON tool where it doesn't (Bedrock Converse, older Anthropic models). The response arrives as ordinary text deltas either way, so consumers see no stream-shape difference.

Routes that can't enforce a schema fail closed rather than silently degrade: the client throws on any provider `responseFormat` warning (DeepSeek's degradation to prompt-injected JSON, or an openai-compatible endpoint without structured outputs), and the DeepSeek client rejects the parameter outright since DeepSeek's API has no strict JSON-schema mode. Posit AI's OpenAI-compatible branch opts into strict schemas so they reach the wire there.

title: Add GPT-6.1 Terra and published Bedrock limits for GPT-6.1 models
description:
This PR adds GPT-6.1 Terra to direct OpenAI model discovery, so that it appears with its display name and correct reasoning-effort levels. It also gives GPT-6.1 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol on Amazon Bedrock the context and output limits AWS publishes for them.

1. **OpenAI discovery.** GPT-6.1 Terra shows as "GPT-6.1 Terra" in both the live model listing and the fallback list used when OpenAI's listing fails. Unlike GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, Terra supports OpenAI's "none" reasoning effort, so it offers Off through Max. Its 1.05M context window and 128K output limit come from the existing GPT-6 rules.
2. **Bedrock limits.** Published limits now come from one table with an entry per AWS model card:
   - GPT-6 Astra: 1.05M context, 128K output (unchanged)
   - GPT-6.1 Terra: 1.05M context, 128K output (previously 1M context, unknown output)
   - GPT-6.1 Sol: 1M context, 131,072 output (previously unknown output)

Bare and dated model IDs, such as `openai.gpt-6.1-terra-2026-10-20`, get the published limits. Other suffixes like `-preview` and unknown future GPT-6 IDs keep the default 1M window with no output limit, so an unverified variant never inherits limits it might not have.

Sources: [OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6.1-terra), [AWS GPT-6.1 Terra](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-card-openai-gpt-6-1-terra.html), [AWS GPT-6.1 Sol](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-card-openai-gpt-6-1-sol.html)

title: Require `catalog.envVars` in `createHeadlessProviders()`
description:
Quick follow-up to #162, which made the ai-config loaders require an environment instead of falling back to `process.env`. This forces hosts that scrub their control variables from `process.env` to pass a snapshot, and prevents a silent fallback that would make them lose the admin tiers without any error.

For the same reason this PR makes the `catalog.envVars` field compulsory in `createHeadlessProviders()`. Downstream, Positron has no scrubbing and simply passes `process.env`, but it does so intentionally.

title: Update agentEngines schema descriptions for live settings
description:
The `agentEngines` description still said engines require Posit Assistant's experimental features and that changes take effect after a restart. Neither is true now: the experimental-features gate was removed in posit-dev/assistant, and Positron and standalone hosts apply `agentEngines` changes live.

### Changes

- `agentEngines`: drop both sentences, keeping "Preview: external agent engines that can run a Posit Assistant conversation in place of its own agent loop."
- `idleSessionMinutes` and `maxLiveSessions`: add "Applies after a restart." These are the only two engine settings read at startup (`startupOnlySettings.ts` in posit-dev/assistant).
- `providers.schema.json` regenerated; its diff is only these three descriptions.

title: Add `/settings-report` to explain provider config and credential sources
description:
This PR lets a host ask the provider libraries which layer decided each provider setting and where each provider's credentials come from, without reading a secret or changing any file. Posit Assistant's new `/settings-report` command uses it to show users why a provider is enabled, disabled, or pointed at a given URL, and why a particular credential is in use. The libraries previously reported the final result only.

For provider configuration, the new explanation reads the same sources a normal load reads (the user's file, admin enforced and default values, environment variables, and host defaults) and replays the real merge. Each value names the layer that won and what the other layers said. It also reports whether each layer's file was found, empty, missing, or invalid, so a missing file no longer looks the same as an empty one. Values are masked unless they're declared safe next to the configuration schema, so a newly added field starts out hidden.

For credentials, a new description says whether a provider's credential comes from the stored sign-in, an environment variable, or a host-managed source. It reports the variable name, file path, and save time, never the value. The description shares its decision with the code that actually fetches credentials, so the reported order is the order used at runtime. Reading the store for the description doesn't repair file permissions the way a normal read does.


## Changes

- JSON parse errors for provider settings in environment variables no longer quote the input. Previously, a malformed value could copy part of a secret into logs. The message now names only the variable.
- A malformed credential store logs fixed wording instead of the parser's message, which quotes nearby text.
- Credentials and account names embedded in URLs, including padded or protocol-relative forms like `//user:pw@host` and Snowflake account values, are removed before a URL is shown.
- A Connect sign-in saved for a different server is reported as such, instead of as a missing sign-in.
- Issues in an explanation say whether the whole source was ignored or only its provider configuration (engine settings can survive), so a report can describe the real consequence.

## Not included

- The explanation doesn't predict the effect of an edit. A layer marked "no effect" means it was shadowed in the current state.

title: Give new Claude, GPT, and Gemini models the latest known limits
description:
When a provider releases a model the capability tables don't list yet, the app guesses its limits, and the guess is often stale. A new Claude Sonnet 5.7, for example, matches an old catch-all rule and gets the limits and thinking levels of Sonnet 5, even though Sonnet 5.5 is already known to be more capable. A new Gemini Flash 3.9 gets a thinking-level picker that offers "minimal", which the newest known Flash (3.8) dropped.

This PR makes an unrecognized model inherit the capabilities of the newest known model in the same tier. `claude-sonnet-5-7` takes Sonnet 5.5's context window, output limit, and thinking levels. `claude-opus-6` takes Opus 5.5's. `gpt-7` takes the newest named GPT flagship (`gpt-6.1-sol`), and `gpt-7-mini` or `gpt-7-nano` takes the newest mini or nano. `gemini-3.9-flash` takes Gemini 3.8 Flash, and `gemini-4-pro` takes Gemini 3.1 Pro. Every provider that reuses the shared tables benefits, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex, OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Portkey, Databricks, Snowflake, and Posit AI Pass.

Adding a model to a table is still a single entry, and that entry becomes the fallback for later versions. Nothing is copied: an inherited result is the donor's own result.

Tiers never mix. A model in a tier with no known entry at or below its version, such as `claude-poet-6` or `gemini-4-ultra`, keeps today's conservative defaults. Older ids keep their existing results, and dated or provider-suffixed ids (`claude-sonnet-5-20260724`, `anthropic.claude-opus-4-8-v1:0`) still match exactly. A date is never read as a minor version.

The hosted Gemini API is stricter. A future model gets the newest profile only when it is at or above that variant's newest profiled version and is a chat model. Older or in-between unprofiled models still get no level picker, because Gemini's level sets are not monotone (3 Pro supports only low and high, and 3.7 Flash dropped "minimal"). Image and speech variants never inherit.

## Changes

- Unknown Claude ids in a known tier now inherit that tier's newest entry. Previously, a broad prefix rule such as "any Sonnet 5" matched them, or they fell to the 200k / 64k default.
- Unknown GPT generations (`gpt-7`) now inherit the newest flagship, mini, or nano. Previously, they got the generic defaults.
- Unknown Gemini variants inherit the newest known Flash, Flash-Lite, or Pro, so `gemini-3.9-flash` no longer offers "minimal".
- The OpenAI live model listing now includes `gpt-<N>` for N of 4 or more, so a future generation appears in the picker before a table update. `gpt-3.5` and `instruct` models stay excluded.
- On the hosted Gemini API, `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` now offers minimal, low, medium, and high, which Google's documentation lists for it. Previously, it offered no levels.
- LiteLLM aliases for a future `gpt-<N>` without reasoning metadata now route through the Responses API, as known GPT-5 and GPT-6 aliases already do.
- The packages move to Vitest 4.1.12 to match the Posit Assistant monorepo. Previously, the monorepo installed a nested Vitest 3 for each package, and running `npx vitest` inside a package silently used the root's Vitest 4. The Vertex test's `GoogleAuth` mock now uses a `function` expression because Vitest 4 no longer lets an arrow function be called with `new`.

## Design decisions

- **Inherit thinking levels too.** An inherited model offers the donor's thinking levels as-is, even when that includes "off". The alternative was to offer no levels, which would make every new model run at its default thinking state. The cost is that a new model may reject a level it doesn't support until a table entry is added.
- **No "inferred" marker.** The context budget already treats table values as hard limits, and the existing catch-all rules already report guesses as table values. A new flag would add a branch downstream for no benefit.
- **Inherit per tier, not per generation.** Limits differ across tiers of one generation (Sonnet 4.6 has a 64k output limit, and Opus 4.6 has 128k). Within a tier they have only grown, so the newest entry is the best guess.

## Not included

- Pricing never inherits. New ids stay unpriced until a rate-card row exists.
- Bedrock Mantle stays conservative, because AWS publishes different GPT limits than OpenAI.
- The o-series, DeepSeek, OpenCode, and Gemma keep their own defaults.

## Verification

Call the capability helpers with a future id and compare against the donor, for example `getAnthropicModelCapabilities("claude-sonnet-5-7")` against `claude-sonnet-5-5`, or `getGeminiModelCapabilities("gemini-3.9-flash")` against `gemini-3.8-flash`. The new unit tests do this for each case above.

title: Force reasoning params on OpenAI Responses when a thinking effort is set
description:
Fixes posit-dev/positron#15967 (cross-ref posit-dev/assistant-feedback#101).

When a user sets a thinking effort on a model served through the `openai` provider, `@ai-sdk/openai` decides whether it is a reasoning model by matching the model ID (`o\d+` or `gpt-5+`). Any other ID is treated as a non-reasoning model, for example Qwen, GLM, `gpt-oss`, a local proxy, or a deployment name behind a custom `baseUrl`. For those models the SDK silently dropped these fields even though effort was set:

- `reasoning: {effort, summary}`
- `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`
- the `developer` role for the system prompt, which was sent as `system` instead

The backend then never reasoned. `BedrockClient` already sets `forceReasoning` for the same reason. `OpenAIClient` did not.

**Change** ([OpenAIClient.ts](packages/ai-provider-bridge/src/model-clients/OpenAIClient.ts)): on the **Responses** route, the thinking branch now sets `forceReasoning: true`. `reasoningSummary: "detailed"` is also set only on Responses, because Chat Completions drops it with a warning.

**Scope.** I did not force reasoning on Chat Completions, even though the issue's diff does. On Chat, forcing also switches the system prompt to `developer` and `max_tokens` to `max_completion_tokens`, which many OpenAI-compatible servers reject. So on Chat, effort for unrecognized model IDs is still dropped. I treated that as a separate decision, so this PR does not fully close the issue. Reviewers should decide whether to close it with this PR or keep it open for Chat. DeepSeek's built-in provider is unaffected because it patches the request body itself.

A new wire test, `openai-force-reasoning-wire.test.ts`, asserts the raw request body.

## How to test

**Automated**

```bash
npm test -w ai-provider-bridge
npm run check-types
npm run format:check
```

**Manual (LM Studio, via the Posit Assistant monorepo)**

The fix only applies when an effort is sent. `ai-config` only knows effort levels for real OpenAI model IDs, so for local models declare them in `~/.posit/ai/providers.json`:

```jsonc
"openai": {
  "enabled": true,
  "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:1337/v1",
  "models": {
    "overrides": {
      "openai/deepseek-r1-0528-qwen3-8b:2": { "thinkingEffortLevels": ["off", "low", "medium", "high"] }
    }
  }
}
```

1. Build this branch in `assistant/packages/ai-lib` and reload the window. An effort picker should now appear for those models. Set it to **High**.
2. Send a message, then inspect the newest request log:
   ```bash
   f=$(ls -t ~/pa-http-logs/*-openai-*-request.http | head -1)
   awk 'b;/^\r?$/{b=1}' "$f" | jq -c '{model, reasoning, include, store, roles:[.input[] | .role // .type] | unique}'
   ```
   Expected:
   - `reasoning: {effort: "high", summary: "detailed"}`
   - `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`
   - `store: false`
   - the system prompt sent with role `developer`
3. Before/after: check out `main`, rebuild and repeat. You should see `store: false` but no `reasoning`, no `include`, and role `system`. That is the bug.
4. Confirm LM Studio accepts the request and reasons. The matching `*-response.http` should start with `200` and contain `response.reasoning` events.
5. Send a follow-up in the same conversation. `store: false` means the client no longer produces `item_reference` inputs, so check that multi-turn still works with thinking on.

If `reasoning`, `include` and `store` are all missing, no effort was sent. That is the `thinkingEffortLevels` gate above, not this change.

title: Add a headless provider entry for Positron

- Adds the `ai-provider-bridge/headless` entry: one factory that watches the provider catalog, reports which sign-in each provider needs, turns a raw session token into provider credentials, lists models with the catalog's model policy applied, and streams chat. It serves the same providers with the same credentials as Positron does today, except for the bug fixes below.
- Model listing reports whether a token produced usable credentials, so Positron can still tell a user to sign in rather than reporting that no model matched.

- LiteLLM, OpenAI-compatible and custom entries of key-optional kinds need no session. Without a stored key they use an empty key with the catalog base URL, as Assistant's chat does. Built-in Portkey still needs a key.
- Posit AI Pass uses the catalog's base URL instead of always using the default gateway.
- Chat uses each model's configured protocol and base URL, as Assistant's chat does, so custom providers on the Responses API and per-model endpoints work.
- With model discovery off, listing sends no `/models` request and returns the configured models.
- A provider error mid-stream rejects the chat instead of ending as an empty or cut-off reply.
- Chat rejects a model that is not in the provider's listing, with the same message as Assistant's chat.

title: Derive Snowflake Cortex models from SQL discovery
description:
The Snowflake model picker now lists the models the user's account can actually use, instead of a fixed list. The bridge runs `SHOW CORTEX BASE MODELS IN SCHEMA SNOWFLAKE.MODELS` through Snowflake's SQL API (`POST /api/v2/statements`) and keeps the rows that are recognized Claude or OpenAI ids and whose lifecycle status isn't `EOL`, `LEGACY` or `INTERNAL`. Cortex has no list-models REST endpoint, so the SQL query is the only way to see what a role can access.

When the query can't run, fails, or yields nothing usable, the picker falls back to a static list of 13 current models (Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku 5.x and 4.8, GPT-6 and 5.6 lines). Every Snowflake model, whether listed, fallback or user-defined in `models.custom`, now takes its context window and output limit from the upstream Anthropic/OpenAI capability tables rather than Cortex-specific windows. Ids those tables don't know keep conservative fallbacks (200k/16k for Claude, 128k/16k for OpenAI).

## How it works

- `createSnowflakeModelFetcher` is rebuilt on `createCachedModelFetcher`, so it gets the shared TTL cache, stale-cache-on-failure and static-fallback policy. Failures aren't cached, and `clearCache` is forwarded. Both the built-in and custom Snowflake registrations share it.
- Auth is the Bearer API key (PAT), or the existing session fetch (exported from `SnowflakeClient.ts` as `createSnowflakeSessionFetch`) when the credentials carry a Snowflake session. Headers merge `customHeaders`, so the token-type header and default User-Agent are carried along.
- The response is parsed by column name (`name`, `lifecycle_status`). Any other shape, including a 202 async response, throws and takes the fallback path.
- `ai-config` now exports the recognition predicate `isRecognizedSnowflakeCortexModel` (a Claude id with an explicit Anthropic-table rule, or an `openai-` id the OpenAI table knows) and a display-name formatter, `snowflakeCortexModelName`. The static catalog shrinks to the fallback ids only.

## Accepted costs

- Older models Snowflake still marks GA (for example `claude-opus-4-7`, `openai-gpt-5.4`) are listed, in SQL row order.
- The query can't tell whether REST serves a model. A recognized model that only works through `AI_COMPLETE` fails with `400 unknown model` when picked.
- A new point release (for example `claude-sonnet-5-7`) appears automatically but inherits the traits of the older sibling rule until a separate cross-provider capability-fallback change lands.
- No per-account cache key. Credential changes already clear all model caches; a connection switch that skipped that would show the previous account's list until the next invalidation.
- SSO session tokens are sent to the SQL API even though support is undocumented. If rejected, those users get the static list at the cost of one failed request per listing.
- One extra SQL request each time a host lists or re-lists Snowflake models.
- Input caps for the 1.05M-window models (GPT-5.4/5.6/6) are unverified. If Cortex caps input below upstream window minus output, long conversations would hit a request error before compacting.
- Private-preview models may still be listed for accounts that aren't enrolled, and grant changes appear only after the listing is refreshed.

## Testing

Unit tests cover the recognition predicate and name formatter in `ai-config`, and in the bridge: filtering by recognition and lifecycle, fallback on HTTP error, malformed body (including the 202 shape) and no usable rows, the exact request URL and statement, Bearer vs session auth, the SQL route in the default-User-Agent wire test, and custom-provider ids being preserved. `memory-bank/aiConfig.md` is updated.

15 `google-vertex-provider` tests in `ai-provider-bridge` fail on `main` too and are unrelated to this PR; the Snowflake test files pass with clean output.

Live verification against a Posit dev Snowflake account with a PAT:

- Discovery listed 28 models: the 13 fallback ids plus 15 older GA or preview models.
- All 15 newly listed models served both plain and tool-calling REST requests (HTTP 200), and chat with GPT-5.6 Sol worked.
- The SQL API accepts a PAT without the `X-Snowflake-Authorization-Token-Type` header.
- Cortex caps `openai-gpt-5-nano` input at 272k tokens, which is upstream's 400k window minus 128k output, so upstream limits match Cortex for the GPT-5 line.
- Session (SSO) auth against the SQL API was not tested; no SSO connection was available.

## Follow-up

A separate PR will add a cross-provider "newest in tier" capability fallback, so point releases no longer depend on older sibling rules.

title: Report an expired AWS sign-in only for real sign-in failures
description:
This PR lets host apps tell an expired AWS SSO sign-in apart from other credential problems, and check the sign-in on demand. It is the library half of the "refuse sends when the AWS sign-in has expired" change in the assistant app.

Today the model-list path reports an expired sign-in for any credential failure on a profile that uses SSO. A user who is offline, with a valid session, sees "sign in again" and cannot fix it by signing in. This PR classifies the failure instead. Only known AWS SDK sign-in wording reports an expired sign-in. Anything else reports the existing "invalid or unavailable" status.

The classifier is a pure function exported from the package root, so apps can use it without loading the AWS SDK. The app's chat error formatter uses the same function, so the model list and chat errors agree.

A new function, `checkAwsSignIn`, resolves a provider's credentials and returns one of three results: `ok`, `unknown` (an error the classifier does not recognize), or `sign-in-required` with the expired-sign-in status update ready to publish. It publishes nothing itself, so a caller can put a time limit on the check and decide afterward what to show.

Status updates now have an optional `userInitiated` flag. A host that receives it shows the prompt again even if the user already dismissed an earlier one, and does not treat the update as evidence from model discovery when it verifies a reconnect. The send-time check sets the flag. Model-list reports do not.

## Changes

- "Token is expired" now counts only with the SDK's "To refresh this SSO session" text. "Returned expired credentials" counts only with the `credential_process` prefix. A helper that prints "OAuth token is expired" or "certificate has expired" is no longer treated as a sign-in problem.
- The classifier recognizes two wordings it missed: the older "The SSO session associated with this profile is invalid" and "Value not present for '...' in SSO Token".
- A credential failure while loading the model list reports an expired sign-in only when the classifier matches. Previously it reported one whenever the profile used SSO.


## Breaking changes

The expired-sign-in status update type is now a named type with the new optional `userInitiated` field. Existing consumers keep working because the field is optional. Consumers that rely on any credential failure on an SSO profile reporting an expired sign-in will now see the "invalid or unavailable" status for unrecognized errors.

title: Report which layer decides each agent engine's enabled flag
description:
This PR makes the shared provider configuration reader report which layer decides the agent engine master switch and each built-in engine's `enabled` flag: the administrator's enforced layer, the user's file, a defaults layer, or none. A product can then tell whether a user's edit can change a flag. Before, an enforced `true` and a user's `true` looked the same as values, so a product could only guess whether turning an engine off would stick.

The answer comes back with the resolved engine block, from the one-time load and from every file-watcher event. The watcher now also fires when only the deciding layer changes. For example, if the user deletes an `"enabled": true` that a defaults layer also sets, the value stays `true` but the deciding layer moves from the user's file to the defaults layer, and listeners hear about it.

When there is nothing to report:

- Only the master switch and the built-in engines (Copilot, Claude, Codex) carry this information. An Agent Client Protocol agent has no flag, because an entry is enabled when it exists.
- A flag that no layer sets is reported as unset, and the product's own default applies.
- The environment layer carries connection fields only, so it never decides a flag.
- A new built-in engine added to the schema gets the same reporting without further changes.

## Example

With `{"agentEngines": {"enabled": true, "claude": {"enabled": true}}}` in the user's file, an enforced layer that sets the master switch, and a defaults layer that sets `codex`, the report says:

```json
{
  "enabled": "enforced",
  "claude": { "enabled": "user" },
  "copilot": { "enabled": "unset" },
  "codex": { "enabled": "default" }
}
```

## Breaking changes

The catalog report and the watcher's change event gain a required field. Code that builds either by hand, such as a test fixture, needs to add it.

title: Move the provider bridge to AI SDK 7 with no change for users
description:
This PR upgrades the provider bridge from AI SDK 6 to AI SDK 7 and bumps its version from 0.0.10 to 0.1.0, so that Posit Assistant and the other consumers run on the current SDK and the current major version of every model provider package (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Vertex, Bedrock, DeepSeek, OpenAI-compatible, OpenRouter, and Ollama). Users should see no change in behavior. The bridge writes no new message shapes, so conversations that older builds can read stay readable.

The upgrade uses only three of the SDK's automated renames: the stream property, the step-finished callback, and the Google provider factory. The system prompt option is renamed by hand at each model call. The SDK's all-in-one upgrade tool is deliberately not used, because it would also rename the system field that the VS Code language model API expects, and it would rewrite image parts into a different shape.

AI SDK 7 accepts a wider set of message content than version 6, and it no longer accepts the older "media" form of a tool-result image. The bridge's converters handle the wider content on the read side: content they can't send (for example, an image that is a provider file reference rather than bytes) is skipped, as other unsupported content already was. The bridge no longer understands "media" tool results, so consumers must convert old ones before sending. The monorepo PR does this per request.

## Is anything translated between AI SDK 7 and 6?

No. The bridge does not convert between the two versions in either direction.

- **Streaming:** `convertAiSdkStreamToPlatform` yields the SDK's v7 stream parts as-is, and `LMStreamPart` is the SDK's own stream part type. The new parts (`custom`, `reasoning-file`) reach the consumer unchanged, and the consumer decides what to do with them.
- **Messages:** the bridge sends v7 messages to the providers without rewriting their shape. It adds no producers of v7-only content. The only changes are on the read side: converters skip content they can't send, and the bridge no longer understands the old "media" tool-result part (consumers convert it first).
- **Not a v6 translation:** the VS Code language model converter (`positron/message-formats.ts`) still turns messages into VS Code API objects, as before. That is a conversion to a different API, not to v6.

## Changes

- Step logging still records request bodies. AI SDK 7 stops including them in step results by default, so the bridge now asks for them whenever a step logger is active. With no loggers, nothing changes.
- Model responses that the bridge builds itself (VS Code language model API) now report step timing as zeros, because AI SDK 7 requires the field and these clients measure nothing.
- Bedrock Mantle requests no longer send the extra web search sources field that the old SDK added. Mantle doesn't support it.
- OpenAI Responses tool definitions now send an explicit non-strict flag instead of omitting it. The User-Agent header now names the SDK's provider utilities package instead of the SDK itself.

## Breaking changes

For consumers of the bridge's exported types:

- The message type gains a reasoning-file content part, and the tool-result "media" part is gone.
- The stream part type gains new members, including provider-specific "custom" events and reasoning files. Consumers that branch on part type need to handle or ignore them.
- The usage type drops its deprecated top-level fields. For example, reasoning tokens are now read from the output token details.

The bridge keeps `ai` as a regular dependency. It needs Node 22 or later, as AI SDK 7 does.

## Not included

- Persisting reasoning files. The bridge streams them, but consumers decide whether to store them.
- Moving to the SDK's canonical file content part for images. That changes what gets written to disk and needs its own design.

title: Report whether a providers.json update changed the file
description:
This PR makes the shared function that updates `providers.json` report whether it actually wrote anything, so that an app can finish a save only when the file changed. It resolves to `true` when the update wrote new content and to `false` when the result was identical to what was already on disk.

Before, the function returned nothing, so a caller could not tell a real change from a no-op. Posit Assistant needs the distinction so it can skip the "provider changed" refresh when a save, such as re-saving an unchanged base URL, leaves the file untouched.

Creating a missing file whose only content is the seed metadata also reports `false`, because no user setting was written. Invalid or unreadable files still reject, as before. Existing callers that ignore the result keep working.

## Changes

- Callers can now read the result of a `providers.json` update. Previously the function returned nothing.
- The in-process write queue now passes each update's result through to its caller. It still runs updates to the same file one at a time.
- The ai-config README, memory-bank notes, and a test cover the new return value.

title: Make an env or admin Snowflake account override a saved endpoint URL
description:
This PR changes how the Snowflake Cortex endpoint is resolved, so that the highest-priority configuration layer decides the endpoint and a lower layer can no longer override it. The endpoint can be given as a full URL, an account name, or a host. Before this change, each of the three was merged separately across layers, and the URL took precedence over the other two. A URL saved in the user's `providers.json` therefore beat an account that an administrator or an environment variable had pinned.

Now the three settings resolve as one. The highest layer that sets any of them wins, and the values from lower layers are dropped for all three. For example, if the user's file has a URL and the `SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT` environment variable is set, requests go to the environment's account rather than the saved URL. If an administrator pins an account and the user later saves a URL, the URL is stored but ignored, like any other pinned field.

Within a single layer, nothing changes: if one layer sets both a URL and an account, the URL still wins. Every layer counts, including the legacy enforced-settings channel that Positron still uses, so callers need no extra knowledge about where a value came from.

This is a prerequisite for letting standalone, RStudio and TUI hosts save the Snowflake URL in `providers.json` (posit-dev/assistant#2763). Without it, those hosts would let a saved URL shadow an administrator's account.

## Changes

- A URL or host saved in a user file no longer overrides an account set through an environment variable or an administrator's configuration. Previously it did.
- A lower layer's URL is no longer combined with a higher layer's account. Previously the URL silently won.
- The `aiConfig.md` resolution notes and the credential-shaping test header describe the new rule.

title: Add agent engine configuration to providers.json
description:
This PR adds an `agentEngines` block to `providers.json`, next to `providers`, so that products can read external agent engine settings (GitHub Copilot, Claude Agent, Codex, and Agent Client Protocol agents) through the same layered reader as providers, including the administrator's enforced and default environment variables.

The reader owns only the shape and the merge; each product applies its own defaults and decides what the settings mean. The resolved block comes back with the provider catalog, and the file watcher reports a change when only the engine block changes. The block is published in `providers.schema.json` as a preview.

How layers combine, and what happens with bad input:

- A higher layer's value wins field by field, so an enforced `"enabled": false` turns every engine off. Unset fields stay unset.
- An agent entry is replaced whole by a higher layer's entry with the same name, so an administrator's command never runs with a user's arguments or environment variables. For the same reason, every agent entry must name its command in every layer; an entry without one is dropped with a warning.
- Invalid fields and entries are dropped one at a time with a warning, and their siblings stay. Engine settings and provider settings are resolved independently: an engine problem never causes a layer's provider rules to be ignored, and a provider problem never discards a layer's engine settings. This holds for sources a caller passes to the resolver directly, not only for ones read from files and environment variables.
- Older readers whose schema predates the block refuse to write a file that contains it, because the root schema is strict. Products coordinate that rollout.

title: Remove the old direct GitHub Copilot SDK implementation
description:
This PR removes the provider bridge's direct GitHub Copilot model client, which sent chat requests through the user's locally installed Copilot command-line tool, so that consumers stop listing or calling Copilot through that path and the bridge no longer depends on the Copilot SDK or bundles the Copilot CLI. This is the Copilot implementation that Posit Assistant in Positron used behind the internal-testing `assistant.enableCopilotSdk` setting (off by default).

Copilot through VS Code's language model API (`vscode.lm`) is unaffected:

- **Vendor mapping still resolves.** Copilot's models arrive under vendor `copilot`, which is itself a known provider id, so the bridge maps it directly without a mapping-table entry.
- **The only alias removed was unused.** The removed table entry also mapped vendor `github` to Copilot, but both Positron Copilot extensions register their models under `copilot`.
- **The client is untouched.** The `vscode.lm` model client and its Copilot-specific handling don't change.

With the direct client gone, the bridge no longer registers a Copilot provider, and Copilot no longer has an entry in the table that tells hosts which sign-in session holds each provider's credentials. Hosts that read that table stop requesting a GitHub token for Copilot automatically, with no host-side filtering needed. The bridge's lockfiles drop the Copilot SDK 0.2.2, the Copilot CLI 1.0.54, and its platform-specific packages.

The removal doesn't touch any stored data:

- `copilot` stays a known provider id in the shared vocabulary and in the providers configuration file schema, so saved model selections and existing configuration files still load.
- The legacy Positron settings migration still translates the old GitHub connection settings to Copilot.

## Breaking changes

- The bridge no longer exports `registerCopilotProvider` or `CopilotSdkClient`.
- Positron's background AI features (notebook ghost cells, Visualize, commit messages) currently use the direct Copilot client as a fallback model source. They lose that fallback once Positron updates its ai-lib pin.
- Posit Assistant already turned this path off in its companion change. Its Copilot support now comes from VS Code's language model API and its separate Copilot agent integration.

## Not included

- The credential layer's fallback sign-in scopes support is now unused, because Copilot was its only user. Removing it also changes Positron core's provider mapping type, so it comes in a follow-up.

title: Keep admin provider rules when env payloads contain unknown settings
Use catalog ids as auth provider ids
description:
**This should not merge until the coordinated effort with Assistant and Positron**

Auth provider ids become catalog ids, so ai-lib, Assistant and Positron use one id per provider. LiteLLM, Portkey, OpenCode and Posit Connect also gain auth mappings.

| Catalog id      | Old auth id      | New auth id         |
| --------------- | ---------------- | ------------------- |
| `anthropic`     | `anthropic-api`  | `anthropic`         |
| `openai`        | `openai-api`     | `openai`            |
| `gemini`        | `google`         | `gemini`            |
| `deepseek`      | `deepseek-api`   | `deepseek`          |
| `positai`       | `posit-ai`       | `positai`           |
| `bedrock`       | `amazon-bedrock` | `bedrock`           |
| `google-vertex` | `google-cloud`   | `google-vertex`     |
| `litellm`       | none             | `litellm`           |
| `portkey`       | none             | `portkey`           |
| `opencode`      | none             | `opencode`          |
| `posit-connect` | none             | `posit-connect-llm` |

`POSITRON_LEGACY_AUTH_PROVIDER_IDS` maps each renamed provider back to its old id for Positron builds whose authentication extension still declares them. The bridge's vscode.lm layer also uses it to resolve language model vendors that those builds register under the old ids.

- The Posit Connect LLM gateway uses `posit-connect-llm`, because Posit Publisher already registers `posit-connect` for deployment credentials.

A consumer that bumps ai-lib past this change reads sessions under the new ids.

title: Send Workbench attribution with Connect model requests
description:
This PR lets Posit Assistant attach Workbench session and project details, along with optional user-defined fields, to model requests routed through the Posit Connect gateway. Connect can then include that context in its usage logs and tracing instead of recording only the caller's identity.

The provider bridge reads the environment fields, validates and percent-encodes their values, and sends the bounded metadata header on Connect chat requests across both Anthropic and Bedrock routes. Missing fields produce no header; invalid or excess fields are dropped with warnings for the host to report. Configured custom headers cannot impersonate the attribution header, and model discovery never sends it.

title: Fix HTTP 400 from Bedrock Mantle after tool calls with empty output
description:
When a user runs a GPT model on Amazon Bedrock with prompt caching, a tool call that returns no output (for example, a shell command that prints nothing) can make the next request fail with HTTP 400. Retrying fails the same way. The request marks the empty tool result as a cache breakpoint, which sends it as an empty text block carrying that breakpoint. Bedrock Mantle rejects this; the direct OpenAI API accepts the same request.

This PR makes sure no cache breakpoint lands on an empty text block in tool output sent to the OpenAI Responses API, on both direct OpenAI and Bedrock Mantle:

1. An empty tool result is sent as a plain empty string with no breakpoint.
2. When a tool result has several parts, the breakpoint moves to the last part with content: non-empty text, an image, or a file (including files referenced by ID). If no part has content, the breakpoint is dropped.
3. A breakpoint placed directly on an empty text part is removed, whatever placed it.

Dropping a breakpoint costs one cache write on the next request; the model's input is unchanged. Text that contains only whitespace still counts as content, because Mantle accepts it. Tool results with content are sent exactly as before.

Part of posit-dev/assistant#2729

## Design decisions

- **Remove the breakpoint instead of adding placeholder text.** A single space passes on both endpoints, but it would make the request differ from the saved conversation.
- **Fix it in the bridge, not in Posit Assistant's breakpoint placement.** Only the bridge knows that an OpenAI Responses breakpoint must sit on a content block. Moving the placement would also change Anthropic and Bedrock Converse requests.
- **Let the OpenAI SDK wrap non-empty tool output.** `@ai-sdk/openai` has wrapped marked scalar tool output in a text block since 3.0.106, so the bridge's own conversion is deleted and the minimum version rises from `^3.0.88` to `^3.0.106`. The lockfile already resolves 3.0.124, so installed versions don't change.

## Verification

New wire tests cover each case above for both direct OpenAI and Bedrock Mantle request bodies, and the existing breakpoint tests pass unchanged. The live check against Mantle happens in Posit Assistant after this PR merges and the submodule is updated there.

title: Request detailed reasoning summaries for OpenAI models on Bedrock
description:
This PR changes the reasoning summary level requested from OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock from "auto" to "detailed", so that Bedrock GPT models request the same summary level as the direct OpenAI provider and the thinking text users see is consistent across the two.

#111 switched Bedrock to "auto" in September, after Bedrock rejected explicit summary levels for GPT-5.6 Sol and returned no summary text at any level. [Bedrock added reasoning summary support for all OpenAI models](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/amazon-bedrock-reasoning-summaries-openai/) on 2026-10-09. Live probes in us-east-1 found that all nine GPT models accept every summary level, and "auto" and "detailed" produce summaries of similar length.

Summaries remain at the model's discretion on each request. A response can contain reasoning but an empty summary; the chat then shows no thinking block, and the reasoning is still sent back on the next request so multi-step tool use keeps working. If Bedrock starts rejecting explicit levels again, switching back to "auto" is a one-line change.

## Changes

- Bedrock's OpenAI route now requests "detailed" summaries. Previously it requested "auto".
- A new wire test streams a reasoning summary whose encrypted content arrives only at the end of the reasoning item (as it does live with storage disabled), then checks that the next request sends back the same reasoning item ID, summary text, and encrypted content.

## Verification

In the standalone app, with Bedrock GPT-6.1 Sol at High effort, a hard arithmetic prompt shows a thinking block with summary text, and a two-turn conversation with several code-execution tool calls completes without errors. GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Sol, and GPT-6.1 Sol all accept "detailed" when called directly; GPT-5.6 Sol omits the summary more often than the others under both levels.

title: Identify Posit Assistant in Bedrock, Vertex, and local model requests
description:
This PR adds the Posit Assistant product User-Agent to every chat and model-list request sent to Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Ollama, and LM Studio, so that administrators can tell Posit Assistant traffic apart from other tools, for example by searching CloudTrail for `PositAssistant`. (Direct providers that use API keys have sent this identity since #113; these four did not, because their credentials had nowhere to carry the header.)

A Bedrock chat request now arrives with a User-Agent like this, the same format the other providers already use:

```
PositAssistant/1.4.1 posit_positron/2026.10.0 (linux) ai-sdk/amazon-bedrock/4.0.165 ...
```

The provider registry already adds the product identity before it sets up each request. It now does this for every kind of credential except OAuth sign-ins, so a future credential type gets the identity by default. Each of the four providers passes the header through to both its chat client and its model listing. The change applies to every host that uses the bridge: Positron, RStudio, the TUI, standalone, desktop, and Connect.

Edge and fallback behavior:

- A User-Agent that a user or administrator sets explicitly still takes precedence, as before.
- The official Ollama client replaces any User-Agent it is given with its own. The product identity is therefore added just before the request leaves, ahead of Ollama's `ollama-js/...` token rather than replacing it.
- AWS SDK model listing accepts only a user-agent suffix, and it escapes spaces and parentheses. Those discovery calls carry a normalized form such as `PositAssistant/1.4.1-posit_positron/2026.10.0--linux-`, which still matches a search for `PositAssistant`.
- The header is never saved with stored AWS credentials. Saving now copies only the documented AWS fields, so a credential that carries the header can't write it to disk.

Part of posit-dev/assistant#2685

## Verification

New wire tests capture the outgoing request on each route and check the URL, the request count, and the product token: Bedrock Converse, Bedrock Anthropic, Mantle chat and responses, AWS SDK model listing, Mantle model listing, Vertex Gemini and Anthropic chat, Vertex model listing, Ollama chat, Ollama model list and model details, and LM Studio chat and model list. Each test also checks the authorization scheme, which confirms the request took the intended auth path.

Unit tests can't prove that Bedrock still accepts the signed request with the added header. A live Bedrock call from Positron is still pending and will happen before this merges.

## Not included

- Copilot and external agent engines (Claude Agent SDK, Codex, ACP): their own processes send the requests.
- User-configured custom headers for Bedrock, Vertex, and local providers: the transports would now honor them, but passing them through from the provider config is a separate feature.
- An administrator-supplied User-Agent suffix (the optional ask in posit-dev/assistant#2685).

title: Let hosts drop mismatched Claude thinking instead of erroring
description:
This PR lets a host ask Anthropic to drop earlier Claude thinking that no longer matches the prompt, instead of failing the request. Newer Claude models (Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5) tie each block of earlier thinking to the prompt that produced it, and accounts created on or after 2026-08-31 get a 400 error when the prompt changes between turns.

A host now passes one of three policies with each chat request: `drop_block` (drop mismatched thinking and continue), `error` (fail, for reproducing the problem), or `header-only` (send only the beta header, so Anthropic reports mismatches without enforcing anything). The library sends the setting only when adaptive thinking is on, never next to disabled or default thinking, and applies it to every Claude route: direct Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, Posit AI and Snowflake.

A per-route exclusion list skips routes that reject the beta header. It currently lists only Posit AI, whose gateway returns 400 "disallowed Anthropic-Beta value" until it allows the header. Posit AI requests carry no drop protection in the meantime.

Raw HTTP log file names now include the request's session id (`-session.<id>`), so offline tools can group interleaved requests by conversation. Request bytes are unchanged.

## Verification

Checked live with Haiku 5.5 after changing the prompt between turns:

- Direct Anthropic: `drop_block` returns 200 and reports the dropped thinking; `error` returns 400 ("bound to a different conversation"); `header-only` returns 200 and reports an allowed mismatch.
- Bedrock: the beta moves into the request body; `drop_block` and `header-only` both return 200 with the reports.
- Posit AI: the gateway rejects the beta, so the exclusion applies and requests succeed with thinking replayed.
- Vertex is unverified (no credentials), and the SDK notes that Vertex does not support beta headers. If it fails, add it to the exclusion list.

## Breaking changes

The helper that built Anthropic provider options is replaced by one that takes the host's policy. Hosts that don't pass a policy get the previous behavior.

The assistant monorepo PR that consumes this branch needs it merged first, and its submodule pointer updated if the commit hash changes.

title: Add hosted web search for Gemini, OpenAI, and Bedrock Mantle
description:
This is needed for https://github.com/posit-dev/assistant/pull/2364.

This PR adds provider-executed web search to three model clients, so applications built on ai-lib can offer server-side search with streamed, clickable citations instead of routing every lookup through a local fetch tool:

1. Google-hosted Gemini models can attach Google Search grounding. Only an explicit list of verified Gemini 3.x models advertises the capability — discovery stays optimistic about new models, but the search toggle does not, because Gemini 2.5 rejects built-in search combined with function calling (confirmed against the live API) and unverified models could fail loudly or answer without grounding.
2. The OpenAI client can attach the hosted `web_search` tool on the Responses API, and the Bedrock client can attach the same tool for supported GPT models on the Bedrock Mantle Responses route, through one shared helper.
3. The model catalog now computes the final "supports web search" flag only after configuration overrides and routing are resolved, so every host makes the same decision from the same inputs.

For Mantle, requests always carry an explicit `external_web_access` boolean — whether a cache miss may fetch a live external page. AWS defaults an omitted value to `true`, which would silently widen the egress boundary and can also trip IAM policies that grant Search and Fetch but not external access, so the new (optional, backward-compatible) request parameter defaults to `false`.

Requests that ask for search on a route that cannot provide it — Chat Completions, Databricks MLflow Responses, Bedrock Converse or Anthropic Messages, Mantle Chat Completions — are rejected before any network call rather than silently dropping the capability. Custom OpenAI endpoints require an explicit per-model opt-in; redirected built-in OpenAI endpoints default off. Redirected built-in Gemini endpoints and custom Gemini providers never advertise search, because the Gemini client hardcodes Google's hosted Interactions wire contract. Mantle search additionally requires a documented GPT model family, a web-search-enabled AWS region, and a known non-FIPS transport — an unknown FIPS state withholds the capability rather than advertising a request that transport resolution may later veto. A local tool that occupies the provider tool's reserved name is rejected with a diagnostic naming both tools instead of being silently overwritten.

## Design decisions

- **Capability is gated on the resolved endpoint, not the registrar that discovered the model.** Built-in Gemini credentials can carry a redirected base URL, so "the built-in registrar ran" is not evidence that Google's endpoint will serve the request. The same finalization seam applies OpenAI's canonical/redirected/custom rules and Bedrock's model, region, route, and FIPS gates, and an explicit opt-in can never bypass service-side gates.
- **One merge helper owns the provider-tool key reservation.** Both the Anthropic `web_search` merge (pre-existing) and the new OpenAI and Google merges go through it, which fixes a silent-overwrite bug: previously a local tool named `web_search` would have been replaced without any error.
- **The verified-model list for Gemini is deliberate.** Being conservative costs a one-line addition per verified model; being optimistic would hand a broken toggle to every future discovered model.
- **Provider-tool merges are computed before cancellation registration in the OpenAI and Bedrock clients**, so a synchronously rejected name collision cannot leak the abort subscription.

## Not included

- Vertex and custom Gemini endpoints report no search capability; the Vertex client would need its own implementation first.
- A failed Gemini search renders as an empty successful result: the pinned `@ai-sdk/google` drops the wire's `is_error` flag before emitting the tool result, so no consumer can detect the failure until that upstream fix lands.

## Verification

Wire-level tests capture the actual request bodies: Google Search serialized as `tools: [{ type: "google_search" }]` on the Interactions API (search-only and search-plus-function-tool shapes, which differ in `tool_choice` handling), `{ type: "web_search" }` with OpenAI defaults on the Responses API, and SigV4-signed Mantle requests with `external_web_access` serialized as both `false` and `true`. Capability tests cover the override, route, endpoint, model-family, region, and FIPS boundaries. The Gemini and OpenAI paths were also smoke-tested live, with grounded answers and citation payloads captured via raw HTTP logging.

title: Add Claude Haiku 5.5 and honor Claude thinking Off
description:
This PR adds Claude Haiku 5.5 to model discovery and capability inference so applications can offer its 1M-token context window, 128K-token output limit, and supported thinking levels. It also makes Claude's “Off” thinking setting disable thinking on models that support it, instead of leave adaptive thinking enabled by default.

The provider library updates the Anthropic, Vertex, and Bedrock SDK minimum versions together and uses one thinking-options implementation across Anthropic, Bedrock, Google Vertex, Snowflake, and Posit AI Pass. Active effort levels request adaptive thinking with visible summaries; provider-default requests leave the thinking mode and effort unspecified. Existing route-specific tool-streaming options remain intact.

Haiku 5.5 offers “off,” “low,” “medium,” “high,” “xhigh,” and “max.” “Off” sends an explicit disable request without an effort value, avoiding the incompatible combination of disabled thinking and the highest effort levels. Claude models that cannot disable thinking still do not offer “Off.” Model metadata recognizes bare IDs and supported provider prefixes, and Vertex displays the undated model as “Claude Haiku 5.5.”

Availability still depends on the provider. Snowflake's catalog is unchanged because Cortex does not list Haiku 5.5; the Posit AI Pass gateway is not assumed to serve it merely because the capability rule exists.

## Verification
